items.title: Fuel line fitting
items.summary: An improperly connected fuel-line fitting could come apart and spill fuel.

items.title: Certification label ratings
items.summary: Gross weight ratings and tire pressures on the label were wrong.

items.title: Accelerator cable bushing
items.summary: Bushing could disconnect from the accelerator lever, returning the engine to idle.

items.title: Parking brake pawl
items.summary: Pawl may be improperly hardened and yield under load.

items.title: Steering linkage couplers
items.summary: Couplers left too long in an acid-etching bath could be out of tolerance.

items.title: Intake-manifold stud chafing fuel hose
items.summary: A stud on the intake manifold could chafe the fuel supply hose.

items.title: Brake booster vacuum reservoir
items.summary: Reservoir canisters could leak after a bumper impact.

items.title: Throttle position sensor high idle
items.summary: TPS malfunction could cause intermittent high idle right after starting.

items.title: Salt-belt front rotor corrosion
items.summary: Front rotors in salt-belt states could corrode and separate from the hub.

timeline.change: Unveiled in August at the MGM Grand, Las Vegas, for MY1986: XJ-based, long bed only, 2.5 I4, 2.8 GM V6 or 2.1 Renault turbodiesel; $7,049 base 2WD
Short bed (113 in wheelbase) added; 4.0 I6 (173 hp) replaces the V6; AW4 auto; NP231/NP242; Chrysler buys AMC in March; diesel dropped
Eight-slot grille; 4.0 rated 177 hp; Eliminator trim and Olympic Edition
Aisin AX-15 five-speed replaces the Peugeot BA-10/5 mid-year

Chrysler engine management replaces Renix; 4.0 'High Output' 190 hp; Chrysler 8.25 rear appears; no automatic with the 2.5. The 1991–92 HO is the one to buy: easier to diagnose than the Renix 4.0, which is why Off Road Xtreme recommends the HO in the XJ that shares the engine
Final year; production ends June 12, 1992 after 952 trucks built that calendar year

identify.intro: Every MJ looks alike from the doors forward, so the details are in the bed length, the axle and the VIN. Metric Ton trucks and 4.0 HO trucks are worth more, and sellers often don't know what they have.

items.head: Metric Ton package
items.body: Long-bed only: heavier leaf springs, wheels and tires and a Dana 44 rear axle, rated at 2,205 lb payload. NAXJA members say to ask for it by name and confirm the Dana 44.

items.head: Rear axle cover
items.body: Per NAXJA, an oval cover usually means a Dana 35 and an angular, roughly hexagonal cover means a Dana 44. 1991–92 trucks may have the Chrysler 8.25 (Quadratec lists 27-spline 8.25 lockers for them). Offroaders lists an AMC 20 as a 1986 heavy-duty option.

items.head: Bed length
items.body: Short bed: 6 ft on a 113 in wheelbase (1987–92). Long bed: 7 ft on 119.9 in (1986–92). Per Comanche Club, the Eliminator, Chief and SporTruck were short-bed only and the Laredo long-bed only.

items.head: Renix or HO
items.body: 1987–90 4.0s have Renix management; 1991–92 trucks are the 190 hp 'High Output' with Chrysler controls. 1986–87 grilles have ten slots and 1988–92 grilles eight.

items.head: VIN
items.body: NHTSA's free vPIC decoder reads MJ VINs, including drive type and bed length on early trucks. The tenth character is the model year (G = 1986 through N = 1992). AMC-era VINs start 1JT and Chrysler-era 1989–92 VINs start 1J7. Comanche Club keeps a VIN registry.

capability.v: 18 US gal (68 L) short bed · 23 US gal (87 L) long bed

values.intro: Cheap but rising slowly. Clean, rust-free 4x4 five-speed 4.0 trucks, especially Pioneers and Eliminators, bring the money; rusty 2WD trucks and 2.5s don't.
values.note: Based on 12 Bring a Trailer sales from October 2025 to October 2026 (median $12,600, range $5,100–27,000) and 35 BaT sales since 2019. Top: a refinished 1988 Pioneer 4x4 five-speed at $27,000 (2026) and an original-owner 1989 4x4 at $20,000 (2024).
